zone: Glacier Peak and the DaKobed crest — North Fork Sauk, White Chuck, Suiattle, Buck Creek Pass and the Napeequa
_areas_note: No peak was removed, but the trailhead list needed one correction and one clarification, because the grouping was right about the peaks and wrong about how you reach two of them. THE CORRECTION: the standard way into Clark Mountain and Tenpeak Mountain is the WHITE RIVER road (road 6400, off the Lake Wenatchee end, about ten miles beyond the fork), not Little Giant Pass. Clark's West Ridge / Walrus Glacier goes White River trail to the Boulder Creek trail to a camp at Boulder Pass; Tenpeak goes White River trail to the unmaintained Thunder Creek path and Thunder Basin, or over Boulder Pass and down into the Napeequa. Little Giant Pass off the Chiwawa is a genuine second way into the same valley and is the normal approach for Luahna and Chalangin, but a party sent to Little Giant for Clark has been sent the long way round. White River is therefore treated as a trailhead of this zone. THE CLARIFICATION: Buck Mountain, Mount Berge and Helmet Butte are Buck Creek Pass peaks off the TRINITY trailhead, which entiat-holden.json also touches — but that file covers Trinity only as a road-access and staging story for Fortress Mountain and holds no Buck Creek Pass camp at all, so the high camps for these three are new here and nothing is duplicated. Buck and Berge are additionally reachable from the Napeequa over High Pass, which is what ties the Buck Creek and Little Giant halves of this zone together into one horseshoe rather than two unrelated lists. NOT DUPLICATED from entiat-holden.json: Phelps Creek Campground and the lower Chiwawa River road campgrounds, Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin, Leroy Basin, Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass, Ice Lakes, Holden Village, the Holden ballpark and Holden Lake, Holden Pass. Nothing in this file repeats any of those. Read every entry below against an access picture that is currently the worst in the state: the Chiwawa River road is closed above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, a large 2026 fire closure sits on top of it and also covers the White River road and the Little Giant trail, the Suiattle River road is washed out four and a half miles in, the White Chuck road is gated three and a half miles in and its trail has not existed since 2003, and North Fork Sauk access was badly damaged by the December 2025 storms. On paper this zone has five ways in. In the 2026 season it has closer to none. Sitkum Spire was added after a later pass established it is a feature of Glacier Peak own west summit ridge reached from the White Chuck / Sitkum Glacier side — Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek, already in this file — rather than an upper Sauk objective.

sites.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
sites.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom
sites.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
sites.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.

sites.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
sites.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August
sites.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
sites.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.

sites.name: Glacier Gap
sites.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak
sites.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
sites.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.

sites.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
sites.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party
sites.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
sites.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.

sites.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
sites.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest
sites.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
sites.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old guidebook mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.

sites.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
sites.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass
sites.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
sites.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.

sites.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
sites.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there
sites.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
sites.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.

sites.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
sites.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites
sites.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
sites.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.

sites.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
sites.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties
sites.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
sites.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
